html:
The Western Xia, or Xixia, was an empire of the Tangut people in northwest China from 1038 to 1227. At its height it ruled about a million square kilometres, from the Ordos to the Gansu corridor, with its capital at Xingqing, now Yinchuan.

The Tangut leader Li Yuanhao declared himself emperor in 1038. Xixia sat astride the Hexi Corridor, the road between China and Central Asia, and lived from trade, herding and irrigated farming. It fought and traded with the Song to the south and the Khitan Liao to the east.

The state had its own Tangut script, created in the 1030s, with thousands of complex characters. Its rulers were devout Buddhists and printed large numbers of Buddhist texts.

From 1205 Genghis Khan attacked Xixia again and again. He died during the final campaign in 1227, and the Mongols destroyed the state and much of its people. The empire was nearly forgotten until the Russian explorer Pyotr Kozlov dug up a library of Tangut books at the ruined city of Khara-Khoto in 1909. It was one of the first victims of the Mongol conquests.
